titre: “I Think, Therefore I Am”: Descartes Sets Aside the Syllogism
accroche: The “therefore” in the cogito looks like a deduction. Descartes took the trouble to write that it is not one, and to say why.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1637, in Part Four of the *Discours de la méthode* (*Discourse on Method*), Descartes recounts an exercise: rejecting as false everything that can be doubted. He rejects the proofs of geometry, since people sometimes err in reasoning, and all the thoughts that come to us when awake, since they can also come to us in dreams. Then he writes: “it was necessarily the case that I, who was thinking this, was something.” He holds this truth, “I think, therefore I am,” to be “so firm and so certain” that the most extravagant suppositions of the skeptics cannot shake it, and he adopts it as the first principle of the philosophy he was seeking.

## A “Therefore” That Is Not One

The “therefore” invites us to read a piece of reasoning. A syllogism draws a conclusion from two premises, one of which is a general rule, the major premise: everything that thinks exists; now, I think; therefore I exist. Descartes himself set this reading aside. In his replies to the Second Objections, in 1641, he writes that whoever says “I think, therefore I am” does not conclude his existence from his thought by the force of some syllogism. If he deduced it, he explains, he would have had to know beforehand the major premise, “Whatever thinks is, or exists.” But it is the other way around: this major premise is taught to him by what he feels within himself, that it is impossible for him to think if he does not exist. He adds that it is the nature of our mind to form general propositions from particular ones.

The order is thus reversed. It is not the rule that grounds the case; it is the case, grasped all at once, that supplies the rule. One way to understand it: in an exercise where everything is put in doubt, a general rule would itself need proof, whereas the existence of the one who doubts is established in the very act of doubting.

## In the Second Meditation, No “I Think, Therefore I Am”

The Second Meditation (1641) does not contain the formula in this form. Descartes even supposes there a very powerful deceiver who is busy deceiving him always, and he draws from this: “there is, then, no doubt that I am, if he deceives me.” The conclusion is then: “this proposition, I am, I exist, is necessarily true, every time I utter it or conceive it in my mind.” The certainty is that of an act, renewed each time the act is performed. The Latin form *ego cogito, ergo sum*, which everyone cites, also appears in the Principia (1644, I, 7).

This evidence has a limit that Descartes notes at once: “I do not yet know clearly enough what I am, I who am certain that I am.” The cogito establishes that I am; it does not establish what I am.

The “therefore” then signals a connection one sees between thinking and being, not a step in a demonstration. What remains is the “I”: the evidence concerns the act of thinking, and what the one who thinks is, Descartes acknowledges he does not yet know clearly enough.

carte.punch: “I think, therefore I am”: Descartes specifies that he does not conclude it by a syllogism.
carte.idee: In 1641, Descartes specifies that whoever says “I think, therefore I am” does not deduce his existence: he sees it “by a simple inspection of the mind.” To deduce it, he would have had to know first the rule “whatever thinks exists.”

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A secondary source for the Latin form in the Principia (I, 7), Augustine's “si fallor, sum,” which Descartes acknowledges in a 1640 letter, and Gassendi's objection about the “I.”

quiz.question: Why does Descartes refuse to see “I think, therefore I am” as the conclusion of a syllogism?
choix: Because a syllogism can only conclude to truths of geometry, never to an existence
Because he would first have to know the rule “whatever thinks exists,” which is drawn from the case
Because the premise “I think” remains uncertain as long as the deceiver is not ruled out
Because doubt also reaches logic, which makes any conclusion impossible
quiz.explication: Descartes explains that, if he deduced his existence, he would have had to know beforehand the major premise “whatever thinks exists”; yet this rule is taught to him by the particular case, which he sees all at once. A syllogism can conclude to an existence. And the premise “I think” is not shaken by the deceiver: if he deceives me, then I am. Finally, doubt does not forbid this evidence; it produces it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Descartes conclude in the Second Meditation, faced with the hypothesis of a very powerful deceiver?
choix: That the deceiver cannot exist, since his existence would imply a logical contradiction
That reason must first establish the major premise “whatever thinks exists” before concluding
That the proposition “I am, I exist” is necessarily true every time he thinks or utters it
That the formula “I think, therefore I am” is stated there for the first time in this form
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Descartes writes that “this proposition, I am, I exist, is necessarily true, every time I utter it or conceive it in my mind.” The deceiver, far from threatening this certainty, produces it: if he deceives me, then I am. And the French formula does not appear in this text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the cogito not establish, by Descartes's own admission?
choix: What I am, I who think (my nature)
That I really think, as opposed to dreaming that I think
That the act of thinking necessarily presupposes a subject who thinks
That the certainty of the cogito is renewed every time it is stated
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Descartes writes: “I do not yet know clearly enough what I am, I who am certain that I am.” The cogito establishes that one exists, not what one is. The other three points are, on the contrary, what the text says the cogito has established.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what basis does the entry state that the Latin formula “ego cogito, ergo sum” appears in the Principia (1644, I, 7)?
choix: On a direct rereading of the Latin text of the Principia, reproduced in a note
On Descartes's own quotation in the replies to the Second Objections
On the 1824 Victor Cousin edition, consulted via Wikisource
On a secondary source (Wikipedia), the Principia themselves not having been consulted
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The source says so: “secondary source, used only for the Latin form of the Principia (1644, I, 7). The Principia were not consulted.” The other options cite texts reread for other passages, not for this Latin formula.
